In the L&D Talks episode, host Hakar Sidik, marketing manager at StudyTube, interviewed Kirsten de Roo, an expert in attracting and retaining employees. De Roo said she runs Puls, a recruitment and selection agency that helps small and medium-sized businesses find suitable staff, and coaches and trains entrepreneurs and managers on recruitment and retention.

Kirsten de Roo discussed her book “De Perfecte Match,” about finding the right people for the right roles and retaining them in a tight labor market. At the time of the interview, the book had been available for two weeks, was in the top 10 of a management-book chart, and was praised for its practical advice.

The podcast cited research that 30% of new employees leave within 12 months. Kirsten de Roo attributed early departures in part to poor onboarding: employers may invest heavily in recruitment but then leave new hires without enough attention, support, or help becoming part of the team.

Kirsten de Roo said a LinkedIn post of hers about a seemingly ideal candidate who left after eight weeks received more than one million views. The post drew responses from employers and employees who recognized the experience of starting a job and feeling lost or disappointed by the reality.

De Roo recommended beginning onboarding during recruitment and selection by setting realistic expectations about the role, team, projects, and company culture. Employers should keep in touch between contract signing and the start date, for example by inviting the new hire to lunch or a team meeting, signing the contract in person, or sending a welcome card.

De Roo recommended a clear onboarding plan, including the first 90 days, with responsibilities shared among the manager, HR, colleagues, and the new employee. A buddy or mentor can answer questions; the plan should cover the employee’s role, procedures, tools such as a laptop, workplace culture, and ways of working.

De Roo said onboarding takes about 90 days on average, though technically complex roles may require longer. Regular check-ins should discuss what is going well, what is not, and what support is needed; their frequency should be adjusted to the individual employee’s needs.

De Roo argued that onboarding is a shared leadership and organizational responsibility, not just an HR task. Leaders should model self-reflection and create a culture where employees can ask questions, give feedback, learn, and make mistakes. Remote or hybrid work makes belonging harder, so she recommended more in-person contact during onboarding.

De Roo said early employee departures can cost up to 1.5 years of salary, including recruitment and salary costs and indirect effects such as lower productivity, extra workload for colleagues, and dissatisfied or lost customers. Her advice to HR and managers was to involve leadership and build a business case showing the costs and benefits of effective onboarding.

De Roo said younger employees can be harder to retain and may commonly change employers after two or three years. She advised employers to understand employees’ values and development needs, offer meaningful growth opportunities where possible, and adjust expectations when those opportunities cannot be provided.

De Roo said onboarding can be standardized for groups in similar roles and supported with digital tools, especially in larger organizations, but it should still be adapted to individual employees. She described combining digital learning materials with physical contact and arranging digital training in the sequence employees need for their roles.
